analysis.one_liner: Bans commercial logging on national forests and other federal lands, replacing it with restoration work and worker retraining.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 94 cosponsors to end commercial logging on federal public lands never received a hearing or a vote, dying in subcommittee when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the commercial timber program on national forests, national parks, wildlife refuges, and Bureau of Land Management lands, phasing out existing contracts over two years. It would have redirected money from the logging program into a new restoration corps, retraining and income support for displaced loggers, permanent payments to rural counties and schools, and grants to help homeowners near forests protect their houses from wildfire. It also would have let any citizen sue to enforce the ban, and it preserved Native American treaty rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who per the bill's cited GAO findings pay far more for the federal timber program than it returns; people who use national forests for recreation; rural counties and schools, whose payments would be made permanent; logging workers, who would get retraining grants, job-search and relocation allowances, and hiring preference in the new restoration corps; and homeowners in fire-prone areas, who would get education and technical help making their homes fire-resistant. Native American treaty rights are explicitly protected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, forest users, rural counties, timber workers

how_it_helps.text: Ends commercial logging and timber sales on federal public lands, with exceptions only for noncommercial personal uses like firewood and, in limited cases, timber for nonprofit low-income housing [S3].
Phases out existing timber contracts over two years and pays timber purchasers for terminated contracts [S2] [S3].
Creates a Natural Heritage Restoration Corps in the Agriculture and Interior departments to restore damaged lands, with hiring preference for workers displaced by the logging ban [S2] [S3].
Provides worker retraining, needs-related income payments, job-search allowances, and relocation allowances for workers who lose logging jobs because of the bill [S2] [S3].
Makes permanent the education, road, and other payments to states and counties under the Secure Rural Schools Act, which otherwise were set to run only through fiscal 2006 [S2] [S3].
Authorizes up to $15 million a year to help owners of homes near federal lands reduce wildfire risk to the structures themselves, based on Forest Service fire research cited in the bill [S3].
Lets any person sue to enforce the ban, and waives federal sovereign immunity for those suits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies lose access to federal timber and would be bought out of existing contracts at taxpayer expense. Logging workers and timber-dependent communities face job losses during the transition, cushioned by retraining funds of up to $80 million the first year and $120 million the third year. The public also bears the cost of contract buyouts, restoration work, and retraining, though the bill caps new appropriations at two-thirds of what logging was costing taxpayers annually.

drawbacks.text: Logging workers and timber-dependent towns would lose jobs and income; the retraining grants and restoration hiring preference soften but do not eliminate that loss, and many workers are in remote areas with few alternative employers [S3].
Ending existing contracts early requires payments or loan forgiveness to timber purchasers, an immediate taxpayer cost before any savings arrive [S3].
Removing federal timber from the market, even though it is under 5% of U.S. timber consumption by the bill's own figures, would shift some harvesting to private and state lands or imports [S3].

The bill's restrictions on fire treatments — no removal of overstory canopy and no road construction even for fuel-reduction projects — reflect one side of a genuine scientific dispute about how best to reduce severe wildfire, and would constrain land managers' options [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most Americans the trade is favorable: the bill's own findings cite GAO reports that the Forest Service timber program costs hundreds of millions more than it returns, and federal timber is under 5% of national consumption, so the economic sacrifice is small and localized while the taxpayer savings and forest protection are broad. The real cost falls on a concentrated group — timber firms and logging communities — and the bill's transition aid, while substantial, cannot guarantee displaced workers comparable jobs. Its tight limits on fire-prevention thinning were the strongest good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and four subcommittees, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Leach, a Iowa Republican, introduced the bill on May 20, 2003 with 94 original cosponsors — 90 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 3 Republicans [S3] [S4].
The Speaker referred it to the Resources, Agriculture, and Education and the Workforce committees the day it was introduced [S5].
On June 3, 2003 it was sent to four subcommittees, including the Forests and Forest Health subcommittee, and executive comment was requested from the Agriculture and Interior departments [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the last recorded action is the June 20, 2003 subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies kept their access to federally subsidized timber sales, and taxpayers kept funding a program that GAO reports cited in the bill said loses hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Rural counties and forests got nothing from the bill's permanent county payments and restoration program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber firms; the logging program continued

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 94 original cosponsors across both parties

for.name: 3 of 226 House Republicans

against.what_they_did: The committee of primary referral never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in the Forests and Forest Health subcommittee until the Congress ended

against.name: Timber and logging industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have ended their access to federal timber and bought out existing contracts; no hearing ever advanced the bill

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 90 of 205 House Democrats signed on versus 3 of 226 Republicans — though the lead sponsor was a Republican, and no chamber ever voted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill ends commercial logging on all federal public lands and pays off existing timber contracts, cutting off a supply the bill's findings say the government sells at a net loss to taxpayers. Federal timber is under 5% of U.S. consumption, so the industry loses a subsidized revenue stream rather than its whole market [S3].
The bill cites Forest Service figures that recreation on national forests generates over 30 times the jobs and income of logging there, and its restoration and protection focus favors that use [S3].

industries.industry: Rural counties and school districts dependent on federal timber receipts
industries.note: The bill makes Secure Rural Schools payments to counties containing federal land permanent beyond fiscal 2006, replacing their dependence on logging receipts [S3].

industries.industry: Ecological restoration contractors and workforce services
industries.note: A new Natural Heritage Restoration Corps may hire private contractors, and Labor Department retraining grants would flow to states, employers, and unions — with hiring preference for displaced loggers [S3].
